editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.161, Definition 10.161.1. It distinguishes N-1 from N-2/Japanese domains by whether integral closure is required to be finite only inside the fraction field or inside every finite field extension.

definitions.text: An integral domain R with fraction field K is N-1 if its integral closure inside K is a finitely generated R-module.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: N-1 domain

definitions.text: An integral domain R with fraction field K is N-2, or Japanese, if the integral closure of R inside every finite field extension L/K is a finite R-module.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Japanese/N-2 domain

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.58 on Noetherian graded rings. The ring-theoretic Noetherian condition applies to underlying ideals, while a graded module's finite-generation condition is homogeneous and requires finite homogeneous generators.

definitions.text: A graded ring A=⊕_{n≥0}A_n is Noetherian if it is a Noetherian ring after forgetting the grading, equivalently every ascending chain of homogeneous ideals stabilizes and each ideal is finitely generated.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.58 introductory convention and graded ideal discussion
definitions.context_hint: Graded commutative algebra: Noetherian graded ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.87, introduction and displayed inverse-limit construction. The source defines inverse systems indexed by the natural numbers and their compatible-sequence limit, not merely an abstract arbitrary diagram.

definitions.text: An inverse system of R-modules indexed by positive integers is a sequence M_1←M_2←⋯ with R-linear transition maps φ_n:M_n→M_{n−1}; composites give coherent maps M_n→M_m for all n≥m.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: inverse sequence of modules

definitions.text: The inverse limit of an inverse system ⋯→M_3→M_2→M_1 is the submodule of ∏_{n≥1}M_n consisting of compatible tuples (m_n), so φ_n(m_n)=m_{n−1} for every n≥2.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: inverse limit of a countable module system

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.135, Definition 10.135.1. It carefully restricts the two complete-intersection notions to finite-type algebras over a field, distinguishing one global presentation from a Zariski-local cover by such presentations.

definitions.text: A finite-type algebra S over a field k is a global complete intersection if some presentation S≅k[x_1,…,x_n]/(f_1,…,f_c) satisfies dim(S)=n−c.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: global complete intersection over a field

definitions.text: A finite-type k-algebra S is a local complete intersection over k if Spec(S) has a cover by standard open affines D(g_i) for which each ring S_{g_i} is a global complete intersection over k.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: local complete intersection over a field

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 26.4, Definitions 26.4.1 and 26.4.4. A closed immersion requires a surjective structure-sheaf map with locally generated ideal kernel, while a closed subspace is induced by such a sheaf of ideals.

definitions.text: A morphism i:Z→X of locally ringed spaces is a closed immersion if its underlying map identifies Z homeomorphically with a closed subset of X, the sheaf homomorphism O_X→i_*O_Z is surjective, and its kernel is locally generated by sections.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: closed immersion of locally ringed spaces

definitions.text: Given a locally ringed space X and a locally section-generated sheaf of ideals I⊆O_X, the associated closed subspace is the support Z of O_X/I with the quotient structure sheaf O_Z whose direct image under Z↪X equals O_X/I.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: closed subspace determined by an ideal sheaf

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.14, foundational definitions of cones, universal limits, cocones and colimits and Definitions 4.14.6–4.14.7 of products and coproducts of discrete diagrams.

definitions.text: For a diagram F:I→C, a limit consists of an object L of C with arrows L→F(i) compatible with every arrow of I, such that each other compatible cone factors uniquely through L.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: limit of a diagram

definitions.text: For a diagram F:I→C, a colimit is an object Q equipped with compatible morphisms F(i)→Q such that every other cocone F(i)→Z factors uniquely through Q.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: colimit of a diagram

definitions.text: The product of a family (X_i) in a category C is the limit of the discrete diagram indexed by its family, with projections to the X_i satisfying the usual universal property.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: product of a family

definitions.text: The coproduct of a family (X_i) in C is the colimit of the discrete diagram indexed by its family, with injections from the X_i satisfying the dual universal property.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: coproduct of a family

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.19 describing the Jacobson radical via intersection of maximal ideals and the characterization that 1−xy is a unit for every y when x lies in the radical.

definitions.text: For a commutative ring R, its Jacobson radical Jac(R) is the intersection of all maximal ideals of R.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Jacobson radical

definitions.text: Equivalently, an element x∈R belongs to Jac(R) exactly when 1−xy is invertible in R for every y∈R.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: equivalent unit test for Jacobson radical

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.11 on finite and finitely presented modules. The source characterizes finite modules through preservation of filtered colimits by Hom and finitely presented modules through Hom commuting with filtered colimits.

definitions.text: An R-module M is finitely generated if there exist m_1,…,m_n∈M such that M=Rm_1+⋯+Rm_n; equivalently there is a surjective homomorphism R^n→M for some finite n.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.11, Lemma 10.11.1 and finite module definitions
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: finitely generated module

definitions.text: An R-module M is finitely presented if and only if for every filtered diagram N_i the canonical map colim_i Hom_R(M,N_i)→Hom_R(M,colim_i N_i) is a bijection.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: finite presentation via filtered-colimit Hom

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.76, Functorialities for Tor. The section proves base-change and long exact sequence results for the previously defined Tor functors, rather than defining a new mathematical object called 'functorialities for Tor'. Its statements remain useful as relation/alternate-characterization evidence.

Read Stacks 10.113, Around Krull–Akizuki. The source proves finiteness and Noetherian properties of certain integral closures of one-dimensional Noetherian domains; the named theorem itself is not a separate mathematical definition.

Read Stacks Set Theory 3.3, which uses the class associated with a formula φ(x,p_1,…,p_n) as notation and defines a proper class as one that is not a set. The presentation expressly treats this informally rather than a new set-theoretic object in ZFC, so formal class ontology needs a framework specified before publication.

Read Stacks 10.153, Definition 10.153.1. The source distinguishes Henselian and strictly Henselian local rings by adding separable algebraic closedness of the residue field to Hensel's simple-root lifting property.

definitions.text: A local ring (R,m) with residue field κ is Henselian if every monic f∈R[T] and every simple zero ā of f̄ in κ lift to a zero a∈R reducing to ā modulo m.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Henselian local ring

definitions.text: A local ring R is strictly Henselian if it is Henselian and its residue field has no nontrivial separable algebraic extensions.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: strictly Henselian local ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.54, Definition 10.54.1, distinguishing an algebra essentially of finite type from one essentially of finite presentation by the finiteness of generators and relations before localization.

definitions.text: A ring homomorphism R→S is essentially of finite type if S is isomorphic to a localization T^{-1}A of an R-algebra A finitely generated over R.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: ring map essentially of finite type

definitions.text: A ring homomorphism R→S is essentially of finite presentation if S is a localization of an R-algebra A that admits a presentation with finitely many polynomial generators and relations.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: ring map essentially of finite presentation

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.53, Definition 10.53.1. The Artinian property is a descending-chain condition on ideals, distinguished from Noetherian's ascending-chain condition.

definitions.text: A commutative ring R is Artinian if every descending chain I_1⊇I_2⊇⋯ of ideals eventually stabilizes.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: Artinian ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.72, Definition 10.72.1. It defines I-depth by supremal lengths of regular sequences and explicitly assigns infinity when IM=M; for a local ring, depth abbreviates depth at its maximal ideal.

definitions.text: For a finite R-module M and ideal I⊆R, depth_I(M) is the supremum of lengths of M-regular sequences whose entries lie in I when IM≠M, and is defined to be infinite when IM=M.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: depth of a finite module relative to an ideal

definitions.text: For a finite module M over a local ring (R,m), the depth of M is depth_m(M), the supremal length of an M-regular sequence of elements in m, with depth(0)=infinity.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: depth over a local ring
